Why did it take so long to let the people know what was clearly obvious & then release this 2 days out from the election & put it behind a paywall @nzherald, how long did Jenée Tibshraeny [Herald’s Wellington business editor, based in the parliamentary press gallery] sit on this badly written story 😏

Election jitters: Traders fear left-leaning Government could worsen cost of living

There are jitters among some traders in financial markets over the prospect of a left-leaning Government worsening the cost of living.

The concern is that more unfunded, untargeted spending, as well as policies aimed at lifting wages without raising productivity, could put upward pressure on inflation.

Some observers are also... worried Labour’s pledge to require the Reserve Bank to target employment as well as inflation could see inflation expectations rise, increasing the possibility of actual inflation rising too.

The finance sector hardly has a reputation for being a cheerleader for the left.

However, one participant believed the prospect of the Green Party playing a large role in a Labour-led coalition heightened the sector’s sensitivity to the election.

“Usually the market overprices these events, but my feeling is that this one will have a bigger negative reaction if there is a change of government, especially if the Greens’ representation is significant,” JB Drax Honoré chief strategist for Asia Pacific, Sean Keane, said.

The Green Party has bold tax-and-spend policies that prioritise social and environmental responsibility over debt reduction.

Its co-leader Marama Davidson had to be corrected last week for wrongly believing the Government paid 1-2% interest on its debt, rather than 4-5%.

Keane believed a left-leaning Government would further weaken the New Zealand dollar, making imports (like fuel) more expensive.

“The New Zealand dollar will sell off sharply as investor appetite diminishes in anticipation of higher taxes and more government interference in the economy. The market will start the process of recalibrating to a higher tax and spend environment, and less focus on inflation,” he said.

As for the impact of a left-leaning Government on interest rates, Keane believed this would send shorter-term rates lower and longer-term rates higher.

He saw the reintroduction of the Reserve Bank’s dual mandate pushing markets to price in a slightly lower Official Cash Rate (OCR), which has a bearing on shorter-term interest rates.

As for longer-term rates, these are more closely correlated with international factors as well as New Zealand Government Bond yields, or the interest the Government pays the investors that lend to it.

Keane believed investors would demand more interest if the left came into power, as it would be seen as a little riskier than the right. This would put upward pressure on bond yields and longer-term interest rates.

If a right-leaning Government was elected, he believed the opposite would happen – bond yields would ease back and the New Zealand dollar would rise.

BNZ head of research Stephen Toplis saw the same forces at play but was less certain about them eventuating.

“A right-leaning Government should not change market pricing,” he said in a note.

“A left-leaning government may (and we stress, may) cause a slightly steeper yield curve if investors ponder the implications of a dual mandate and the downward pressure that might put on short-term interest rates while also contemplating the possibility of slightly looser fiscal policy putting upward pressure on bond yields.

“In reality, we doubt much will happen until investors see the whites in the eyes of whatever new policies might be introduced by whichever Government we vote in.”

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold believed prolonged uncertainty over the make-up of the Government post-election would be enough to weaken the New Zealand dollar.

Like Toplis and Keane, he saw a left-leaning Government putting upward pressure on inflation and bond yields.

However, with consumer and business sentiment proving resilient, Eckhold said the election was “business as usual”.

He noted many of the policies discussed during the campaign were unfeasible and wouldn’t be implemented.

Ultimately, he saw businesses and households getting on with it, and believed the market would take the election result in its stride.

Eckhold didn’t believe market movements would be large in the scheme of things, noting that changes to the oil price, global economic outlook and valuations of tech company shares would have much larger impacts on the New Zealand economy.

As it stands, the New Zealand dollar is very weak at nearly US66c.

In the September quarter, the annual inflation rate was above the Reserve Bank’s 1-3% target range, at 3.7%, while the unemployment rate was high, at 5.7%.

The Government is expected to pay $10 billion of interest this year, with the annual cost set to keep rising.
